result.abstractText: CRISPR-Cas12a molecular diagnostics rely on target-activated collateral cleavage of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) reporters to generate fluorescence signals, yet the mechanisms governing reporter substrate processing remain poorly understood. Here we show that Cas12a trans-cleavage involves both endonucleolytic cleavage and exonucleolytic trimming. We further demonstrate that terminal phosphate modification of ssDNA substrates accelerates substrate cleavage activity and modulates trans-cleavage kinetics, thereby enhancing fluorescence output. Guided by this mechanistic insight, we engineered fluorophore-quencher ssDNA reporters bearing terminal phosphate modifications and identified a 3'-phosphate-engineered reporter that enables faster signal generation and higher fluorescence intensity. Incorporation of the engineered reporter into the CRISPR-Cas12a system enabled the development of Phos-CRISPR (Phosphate-engineered DNA reporters boost CRISPR), a rapid, sensitive, and specific nucleic acid detection platform that achieves results within 20 min, approximately threefold faster than conventional CRISPR assays. Applied to herpes simplex virus 1 detection, the Phos-CRISPR combined with recombinase polymerase amplification achieved a limit of detection of 20 aM and accurately identified clinical swab samples. These findings provide a general framework for understanding Cas12a trans-cleavage activity and establish a mechanistically informed strategy for enhancing next-generation CRISPR diagnostics.

result.title: CRISPR/Cas-Based Molecular Diagnostics for Intestinal Parasites: From Proof-of-Concept to Point-of-Care Testing.

authorAffiliation.affiliation: Department of Medical Laboratory Sciences, Faculty of Applied Medical Sciences, King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah 21589, Saudi Arabia.
Special Infectious Agents Unit, King Fahad Medical Research Centre, Jeddah 21589, Saudi Arabia.

result.abstractText: Intestinal parasitic infections remain a significant global public health concern, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where timely and accurate diagnosis is essential for effective disease management and control. Although conventional diagnostic methods, including microscopy, antigen detection, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR), are widely used, each possesses inherent limitations related to sensitivity, turnaround time, laboratory infrastructure, or point-of-care applicability. Recent advances in clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas) systems have led to the development of highly sensitive and rapid molecular diagnostic platforms suitable for decentralized testing. This review summarizes current applications of CRISPR/Cas-based diagnostics for intestinal and foodborne parasitic infections, with particular emphasis on assays developed for Giardia duodenalis, Cryptosporidium parvum, Clonorchis sinensis, Fasciola hepatica, and Schistosoma spp. Published studies have predominantly employed Cas12a, with additional applications of Cas12b and Cas13a and, more recently, a type I-A Cascade-Cas3 system, generally coupled with isothermal amplification methods such as recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) or recombinase-aided amplification (RAA), enabling highly sensitive detection within 60-90 min using fluorescence or lateral-flow strip readouts. The available evidence indicates high analytical sensitivity and specificity, with several assays demonstrating substantial agreement with conventional molecular methods and potential for point-of-care development. However, current CRISPR-based assays remain limited by dependence on nucleic acid extraction, relatively small clinical validation cohorts, lack of standardized protocols, and the persistence of false-negative results associated with low parasite burdens and pre-analytical variables. Emerging strategies, including simplified or extraction-free sample preparation, one-pot sample-to-answer platforms, and detection of parasite-derived cell-free DNA, may further enhance the clinical utility of CRISPR diagnostics. Overall, CRISPR/Cas-based technologies represent a promising next-generation approach for intestinal parasite diagnosis, although large-scale clinical validation and workflow optimization are still required before widespread implementation in routine clinical and field settings.

result.title: Genomic Exploration of CRISPR-Cas Systems in Raoultella species: Diversity and Architecture.

authorAffiliation.affiliation: Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics, Istanbul Technical University, Istanbul, Turkey.
Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics, Istanbul Technical University, Istanbul, Turkey. yilmazcolakc@itu.edu.tr.

result.abstractText: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein (CRISPR-Cas) systems are adaptive immune mechanisms that protect bacteria against invading mobile genetic elements. They can influence horizontal gene transfer, phage resistance, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dynamics. Although these systems have been investigated in several Klebsiella species, information on historically defined Raoultella species remains limited. In this study, 103 complete genomes representing Raoultella species, currently placed within the broader Klebsiella lineage, were analyzed to characterize the distribution, architecture, and diversity of CRISPR-Cas systems. CRISPR-Cas loci were identified using CRISPRCasFinder and CRISPRone, followed by subtype classification, direct repeat and leader sequence analyses, spacer matching, Cas1-based phylogenetic analysis, and AMR determinant screening. Complete CRISPR-Cas systems were detected in 23 genomes, predominantly in R. ornithinolytica strains. All complete systems were chromosomally located, whereas plasmid-associated orphan CRISPR arrays were observed in selected R. ornithinolytica strains. Two major architectures were identified, with Type I-E being dominant and Type I-F restricted to fewer strains. Direct repeat analysis revealed six consensus sequences, while leader regions displayed conserved AT-rich motifs and strain-specific divergence. Spacer analyses suggested historical interactions with phages and plasmids, particularly mobile genetic elements associated with Klebsiella and other Enterobacteriaceae. Cas1 phylogeny showed subtype-dependent clustering, indicating that CRISPR-Cas evolution does not strictly follow core genome phylogeny. The coexistence of predicted CRISPR-Cas loci and AMR determinants indicates that the presence of these loci does not necessarily preclude the carriage of resistance determinants. Overall, this study expands current knowledge of CRISPR-Cas diversity among the analyzed Raoultella genomes and provides a genomic framework for future functional studies.

journal.title: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications

result.abstractText: Most existing CRISPR/Cas12a methods for small molecules detection employ DNA aptamers as an intermediary, while RNA aptamers remain underexplored. The conventional CRISPR/Cas12 system offers limited programmability due to its partially conserved crRNA sequence. In this study, we developed an aptamer-regulated CRISPR/Cas12a system based on split crRNA. We divided the full crRNA into a crRNA handle segment (RH) and a crRNA spacer segment that is identical to the RNA aptamer sequence of target (RS-Apt). RS-Apt was endowed with dual functions: activating the activity of Cas12a and binding to target small molecules, ingeniously linking non-nucleic acid targets with the CRISPR system. The strong affinity between the target and RS-Apt reduces the amount of RS-Apt available to participate in the CRISPR system, resulting in a decrease in the fluorescence signal of the system. Within 1.5 h, the system for theophylline (TP) exhibited a linear range from 50 nM to 200 µM and a detection limit (LOD) of 2 nM, while the system for tobramycin (TOB) showed a linear range of 200 nM to 100 µM with an LOD of 63 nM. Notably, visual semi-quantitative detection of TP and TOB was achieved via lateral flow strips. Moreover, the system achieved satisfactory recovery and visual detection of TP using lateral flow strips in TP-spiked serum samples. This system can detect different targets simply by changing the sequence of the RS-Apt and activator, without the need for complex sequence design of the chains or large-scale instruments, providing a new strategy for CRISPR/Cas12a in the detection of small molecules.

journal.title: Journal of pharmaceutical and biomedical analysis

result.abstractText: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have been shown to be important regulatory factors in initiation and progression of cancer. However, sensitive detection of lncRNAs remains challenging due to their low abundance, complex structure and susceptibility to nuclease degradation. Among various lncRNAs, MIR155HG has been shown to be involved in the progression of cervical cancer and serve as a potential target for biomarker analysis. Here, we developed an exonuclease-gated CRISPR/Cas12a biosensing platform (E-CRISPR) for the detection of MIR155HG without target pre-amplification. This strategy relies on a bifunctional single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) probe containing both a MIR155HG recognition region and a CRISPR/Cas12a activation region. In the absence of target RNA, exonuclease I (Exo I) degrades the ssDNA probe, thereby reducing background signals. Upon binding to MIR155HG, RNA-DNA hybridization reduces the probe's susceptibility to Exo I digestion and allows the retained probe to activate CRISPR/Cas12a and generate an enhanced fluorescence signal. Under optimized conditions, the E-CRISPR assay achieved a limit of detection of 4.76 pM and a linear range of 4.76 pM to 0.4 nM. The entire assay could be completed within 100 min while maintaining sensitive detection of MIR155HG and showed good sequence specificity and reliable performance in complex biological environment. This exonuclease-regulated CRISPR/Cas12a strategy provides a simple analytical approach for extracellular lncRNA analysis.
